bib.title: Making Pre-trained Language Models Better Few-shot Learners

legacy_report:
SOURCE: "Making Pre-trained Language Models Better Few-shot Learners" (LM-BFF). Tianyu Gao, Adam Fisch, Danqi Chen (Princeton, MIT). ACL-IJCNLP 2021, pages 3816–3830. Code: github.com/princeton-nlp/LM-BFF.

COVERAGE: I read all 60,980 of 60,980 characters: body, Discussion, Appendices A–E (Tables A.1, B.1, D.1, E.1) and the references, which I skimmed for origins. Nothing was skipped.

CLAIMS (most important first)

- claim: Template and label-word choice changes few-shot accuracy a lot. Semantically matched label words do best, swapped label words do worst, and small changes to the template cost more than 10 points on SNLI.
  number: SST-2 92.7 (great/terrible) vs 83.2 (terrible/great), with cat/dog at 91.5 and dog/cat at 86.2. SNLI 77.2 (best template) vs 62.9 (sentences swapped) vs 60.6 (label words permuted).
  setup: RoBERTa-large, K=16 per class, prompt-based fine-tuning, mean (std) over 5 random train/dev splits. This is the Table 2 pilot study.
  quote: "<S1> It was [MASK] . great/terrible 92.7 (0.9) ... <S1> It was [MASK] . dog/cat 86.2 (5.4) <S1> It was [MASK] . terrible/great 83.2 (6.9) Fine-tuning - 81.4 (3.8)"; "<S1> ? [MASK] , <S2> Yes/Maybe/No 77.2 (3.7) ... <S1> <S2> [MASK] Yes/Maybe/No 65.8 (2.4) <S2> ? [MASK] , <S1> Yes/Maybe/No 62.9 (4.1) <S1> ? [MASK] , <S2> Maybe/No/Yes 60.6 (4.8)"; "if we put [MASK] at the end, or swap sentence order, we observe a >10% drop."
  where: p.4 (3820), Table 2 and §4.3.
  note: Bad prompts also raise the variance across seeds: std is 0.9 for great/terrible and 6.9 for terrible/great.

- claim: Prompt-based fine-tuning with auto templates and demonstrations beats standard fine-tuning by up to 30 points (SNLI) and by 11 points on average.
  number: 30% max, 11% average. SNLI rises from 48.4 to 77.5.
  setup: RoBERTa-large, K=16, 15 tasks, 5 splits.
  quote: "achieves a 30% gain on SNLI compared to standard ﬁne-tuning, and 11% gain on average."
  where: p.8 (3823), §7.1.

- claim: Prompt-based fine-tuning with only 32 examples reaches about 90% on most binary sentence tasks. SST-2 reaches 92.7 with the manual prompt, against 81.4 for standard few-shot fine-tuning and 95.0 for full-data fine-tuning.
  number: 92.7 / 81.4 / 95.0
  setup: RoBERTa-large, K=16, manual prompt.
  quote: "Prompt-based FT (man) 92.7 (0.9)"; "Fine-tuning 81.4 (3.8)"; "Fine-tuning (full)† 95.0"; "a RoBERTa-large model achieves around 90% accuracy on most binary sentence classiﬁcation tasks, while only relying on 32 training examples."
  where: p.7 Table 3; p.2 Introduction.

- claim: Automatically generated templates (T5 fill-in-the-blank decoding, then fine-tune and rerank on dev) match or beat manual templates. They help most where writing a manual template is unintuitive.
  number: TREC 84.8 manual vs 88.2 Auto T; MRPC 74.5 vs 76.2; SST-2 92.7 vs 92.3; SNLI 77.2 vs 77.1. QNLI 64.5 manual vs 68.3 auto (Table 3).
  setup: RoBERTa-large, K=16. T5-3B generates templates with beam width about 100.
  quote: "Manual 92.7 77.2 84.8 74.5 Auto T 92.3 77.1 88.2 76.2 Auto L 91.5 75.6 87.0 77.2 Auto T + L 92.1 77.0 89.2 74.0"
  where: p.8 Table 5.

- claim: Automatic label-word search is less reliable than template search. It is better on TREC and MRPC but "considerably worse on SNLI", and it picks some inexplicable words.
  number: SNLI 75.6 Auto L vs 77.2 manual.
  setup: same as above. The search uses top-k vocabulary pruning (k=100), the top n=100 assignments by zero-shot accuracy, then fine-tuning and a dev rerank.
  quote: "Auto L outperforms manual prompts on TREC and MRPC—but is considerably worse on SNLI."; "there are also some mysterious abnormalities (e.g., “Hi” for the “entailment” class in SNLI)."
  where: p.8 §7.2.

- claim: Picking demonstrations similar to the query (SBERT cosine, top 50% per class, one example per class) beats uniform random demonstrations.
  number: SNLI 78.8 uniform → 79.7 SBERT; TREC 85.6 → 87.5; MRPC 70.9 → 77.8.
  setup: RoBERTa-large, K=16, 16 demonstration sets per input, ensembled at inference.
  quote: "Uniform sampling 92.3 78.8 85.6 70.9 + RoBERTa sel. 92.7 79.5 83.4 76.6 + SBERT sel. 92.6 79.7 87.5 77.8"
  where: p.9 Table 7.
  caveat: The authors concede SBERT was trained on SNLI and MNLI. A RoBERTa mean-pool encoder also beats uniform sampling.

- claim: GPT-3-style in-context learning (32 random demonstrations, no weight updates) on the smaller RoBERTa-large often fails to beat zero-shot.
  number: SST-2 83.6 zero-shot vs 84.8 ICL; TREC 32.0 vs 26.2; SNLI 49.5 vs 47.1; MRPC 61.9 vs 45.7.
  setup: RoBERTa-large, manual prompts.
  quote: "“GPT-3” in-context learning does not always improve over zero-shot prediction, likely because smaller language models are not expressive enough to use off-the-shelf like GPT-3."
  where: p.7 Table 3; p.8.

- claim: Ensembling automatic templates matches or beats PET's ensemble of manual prompts, and adding more templates helps further.
  number: MNLI 71.9 (PET) vs 70.4 (same number of auto templates) vs 72.7 (20 templates) vs 75.4 (20 templates with demonstrations). RTE 69.2 vs 73.0 vs 73.1.
  quote: "PPET 71.9 (1.5) 69.2 (4.0) Pours,|Pours| =|PPET| 70.4 (3.1) 73.0 (3.2) ... Pours,|Pours| = 20 72.7 (2.5) 73.1 (3.3) + demonstrations 75.4 (1.6) 72.3 (4.5)"
  where: p.8 Table 4.

- claim: The advantage over standard fine-tuning shrinks as K grows. SST-2 nearly saturates at K=16, and on SNLI the two methods converge around K=256.
  number: K=256
  quote: "until the two converge around K = 256."
  where: p.9 §7.4 and Figure 3.

- claim: Dev-set size matters, so the paper sets |Ddev| = |Dtrain| to stay truly few-shot. A dev set 10 times larger inflates results.
  number: Prompt-based FT on MRPC: 70.2 with no dev set, 74.5 with dev = train size, 80.9 with dev = 10× train.
  quote: "Prompt-based FT SST-2 SNLI TREC MRPC NoDdev 92.1 75.3 84.8 70.2 |Ddev| =|Dtrain| 92.7 77.2 84.8 74.5 |Ddev| = 10|Dtrain| 93.0 79.7 89.3 80.9"
  where: p.13 (3828) Table A.1.

- claim: Prompt-based fine-tuning adds no new parameters and so narrows the gap between pre-training and fine-tuning. A standard classification head adds 2,048 new parameters for binary RoBERTa-large.
  number: 2,048
  quote: "a simple binary classiﬁcation task will introduce 2,048 new parameters for a RoBERTa-large model"
  where: p.3 (3819) §4.

- claim: CoLA is the exception: prompting hurts badly there.
  number: 33.9 (fine-tuning) vs 9.3 (manual prompt), Matthews correlation.
  quote: "Fine-tuning ... 33.9 (14.3)"; "Prompt-based FT (man) ... 9.3 (7.3)"; "CoLA is one interesting exception, as the input may be a non-grammatical sentence which is out of the distribution of L."
  where: p.7–8.

- claim: Results hold for BERT-large but are weaker than with RoBERTa-large.
  number: SNLI 59.2 for BERT prompt-based FT vs 77.2 for RoBERTa.
  quote: "Prompt-based FT 85.6 59.2 79.0 66.8"
  where: p.14 Table D.1.

Variance across seeds: the main table reports std over 5 splits. Std reaches 14–16 on CoLA ("21.8 (15.9)") and is 7.4 on QNLI for auto prompts ("68.3 (7.4)").

LIMITS (as the authors state them)
- "the performance still substantially lags behind ﬁne-tuning with thousands of examples, especially for harder tasks." For example, MNLI gets about 70 few-shot vs 89.8 with full data.
- "just like standard ﬁne-tuning, our results also suffer from high variance."
- The search is hard to expand or generalise from "only approximately 32 examples". It still relies on manual label words for template search and manual templates for label search, which "bias it towards areas of the search space that we might have already imagined."
- The method favours tasks that are fill-in-the-blank style, have short inputs and have few classes. Structured prediction is left open.
- SST-2 and SNLI were used for model development, so results on those two are not true few-shot.
- Auto templates can contain "biased peculiarities", and the authors cannot explain why some label words work (App. E).
- Dated: the method requires fine-tuning a masked LM (RoBERTa-large, 355M). The "GPT-3 ICL" baseline runs on RoBERTa, not GPT-3. The findings on prompt sensitivity and demonstration selection carry over to modern LLMs only by analogy. The paper does not test instruction-tuned or decoder-only chat models.

BUILDS ON: GPT series (Radford et al., 2018, 2019; Brown et al., 2020) for prompting and in-context learning. PET (Schick and Schütze, 2021a,b) for prompt-based fine-tuning and cloze patterns. Schick et al. (2020) for automatic verbalizer search. AutoPrompt (Shin et al., 2020) and Jiang et al. (2020) for prompt search. T5 (Raffel et al., 2020) for template generation. SBERT (Reimers and Gurevych, 2019) for demonstration selection. Mettes et al. (2019) for regression as an interpolation between two poles. Dodge et al. (2020) and Zhang et al. (2021) for fine-tuning instability.

CODE: No code listings in the paper. The load-bearing artefacts are prompt formats:
- The T5 template-generation inputs (p.6, §5.2): "<S1>−→ <X>M(y) <Y> <S1>, <S1>−→ <S1> <X>M(y) <Y>, <S1>, <S2>−→ <S1> <X>M(y) <Y> <S2>."
- An example prompt (p.3): "xprompt = [CLS] x1 It was [MASK] . [SEP]"
- An implementation detail (App. C.2): "we prepend a space for label words in M(Y). For example, we use “ great” instead of “great” in the RoBERTa vocabulary". This shows how sensitive the method is to tokenisation details.

FIGURES
- Figure 1, p.2: MLM pre-training vs standard fine-tuning vs prompt-based fine-tuning with demonstrations. One picture shows why reusing the MLM head beats adding a new classifier head, and how the demonstrations are concatenated.
- Figure 2, p.6: the template-generation pipeline (training examples → T5 fills <X>/<Y> → candidate templates → fine-tune and pick the best). Good for 08-prompt-optimization: it shows generate, then evaluate, then select.
- Figure 3, p.9: accuracy vs K for SST-2 and SNLI, fine-tuning vs LM-BFF. Shows where the few-shot advantage closes.
- Table 2, p.4, is a table rather than a figure, but it is the strongest visual for prompt sensitivity (great/terrible 92.7 vs terrible/great 83.2). It is worth rebuilding as a slide.

Note-fit hints: Tables 2, 5 and 6 and §5 (auto search) map to 08-prompt-optimization. §6 and Table 7 (one demonstration per class, similarity-selected, ensembled over 16 sets) and the Table 3 ICL row map to 03-core-techniques.

PROBLEMS: The extraction was clean apart from minor ligature and spacing noise ("ﬁne", "ﬁ"). Math in Eqs. 1, 3 and 4 is garbled, so I did not quote it. Typos in the source ("netural", "real-wold") are copied as printed. There were no embedded instructions.
